text: Everything so far in this chapter -- the Automation Rule, the playbook, the enrichment steps -- was safe to run unattended because nothing changed real-world state. Containment is different. This lesson builds the two containment actions this course treats as real, and the approval gate that has to sit in front of both of them.

Disabling a user account sets accountEnabled to false via Microsoft Graph, which blocks new sign-ins and revokes existing sessions on the next token refresh. Isolating a device, through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, cuts the machine off from the network while leaving Defender's own management channel intact. Both are one API call away from the playbook, which is exactly why they're dangerous to fire unattended.

Go back to the test from Lesson 9: if this automation is wrong, who notices, how fast, and what does it cost? For enrichment, the cost of a mistake was reading an extra line of context. For these two actions, the cost is locking out a real employee mid-shift, or isolating a domain controller and causing the exact outage you were trying to prevent.

The gate itself is a Teams adaptive-card approval step: the playbook posts the proposed action and waits. A Condition then checks whether the response equals approve, and only that branch can reach Disable_user_account. There's no path from incident creation to a disabled account that skips a specific person clicking Approve.

A rejection isn't a dead end either -- it still writes a comment recording who declined it and why, so the incident shows a human looked and chose not to act. Either way, Log Analytics keeps the full run history: who decided, when, and what actually executed.

That's the whole chapter's model, end to end: an Automation Rule triggers a playbook, the playbook enriches the incident automatically, and anything with real blast radius stops at a human before it executes. Next chapter turns to threat intelligence automation -- pulling, scoring, and feeding IOC feeds back into your detections.
